s1.titulo: Age matters as much as the price
s1.texto: With inflation, a price from two months ago doesn't say much. That's why birrapp never shows a price without telling you when it's from.

rancio.nota: Take it as a rough reference.

s2.titulo: Why the cheapest doesn't always come first
s2.texto: When sorting by “cheapest”, prices older than 45 days are ignored. An old, cheap price can't beat a recent, honest one: it would send you across town for a number that no longer exists.

s3.titulo: “Still the same” is the most useful button
s3.texto: Confirming a price hasn't changed takes one tap and makes it fresh again. If nobody confirms, the whole map gets old.

s4.titulo: Pin color goes from cheap to expensive
s4.texto: Lime is the cheapest on your screen and coral the most expensive; in between is each bar's place within that range. The scale readjusts as you move, so the color always speaks about the neighborhood you're looking at, not the whole city.

s5.titulo: The little dot inside is freshness
s5.texto: Inside each badge, to the left of the number, there's a dot in the color of the scale above: it tells you when that price is from. It sits on a dark square precisely so it stands out from the background, which is from the same color family but means something else. You'll never see a price without that dot.

s6.texto: A dimmed dot is something else: it's a bar nobody has added a price for yet. It's not at the expensive end of the scale, it's off the scale.

s7.texto: The initial base comes from OpenStreetMap, and the community adds the missing ones. Prices are always added by people: none are estimated or calculated by us.
